name: BLAKE3
baseline: OpenSSL SHA-256 and SHA3-256 (also MD5, SHA-1 in same chart); BLAKE2b via the blake2b_simd crate
workload: Single-threaded hashing throughput of a 16 KiB input, measured with `cargo bench '16384$'` (criterion)
claimed_speedup: 6866 MiB/s (BLAKE3) vs 484 MiB/s OpenSSL SHA-256 (~14.2x) and 394 MiB/s OpenSSL SHA3-256 (~17.4x); vs 1312 MiB/s BLAKE2b (~5.2x) (derived from page data: ratios computed from the published MiB/s figures)
compiler_and_flags: rustc via `cargo bench` (criterion, release mode); exact rustc version/flags not stated; RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" was applied only to the BLAKE2 comparator, not to OpenSSL
hardware: AWS c5.metal, Intel Xeon Platinum 8275CL (Cascade Lake-SP)
stars_or_usage: 6.4k stars; used in OpenZFS, Cargo, Chia, Solana, Nix, LLVM, ccache, Mold
tradeoffs: Reference/optimized implementation is Rust; the official C implementation (SSE2/SSE4.1/AVX2/AVX-512/NEON, in c/) has a plain C API usable directly from C++. BLAKE3's tree-hash construction gives different streaming/parallelism properties than SHA-2/3 or BLAKE2 and it is explicitly not for password hashing.
caveats: Numbers are hard-coded from the project's own repo benchmark script; hardware and CPU model are stated but exact rustc version/compiler flags used for the comparison are not. The BLAKE2 comparator got an extra target-cpu=native flag not given to the OpenSSL baselines, slightly inflating BLAKE3's apparent lead over BLAKE2b.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3 (seed query variation 'BLAKE3 hash in:name'), then BLAKE3-specs repo benchmarks/bar_chart.py

name: KangarooTwelve (XKCP)
baseline: OpenSSL SHA3-256/SHAKE128/SHAKE256 (FIPS 202); OpenSSL SHA-256/SHA-512 (ARM hardware comparison)
workload: Long-message, single-core XOF/hash throughput in cycles/byte, on x86 with AVX2/AVX-512 and on Apple A14/M1 using ARMv8-A SHA-3 hardware instructions
claimed_speedup: KT128: 1.4 cycles/byte (AVX2), 0.51 cycles/byte (AVX-512), roughly 2x faster than SHAKE128; on Apple A14/M1 with ARMv8-A crypto instructions, KT128 reaches 0.75 cycles/byte, ~1.7x faster than hardware-accelerated SHA-256 and ~3x faster than hardware-accelerated SHA-512
hardware: Unspecified 'current Intel architectures' with AVX2/AVX-512; Apple A14 and M1
stars_or_usage: 664 stars; official Keccak-team code, basis for the SHA-3/Keccak reference and optimized implementations used across the ecosystem
tradeoffs: KangarooTwelve (12-round Keccak-p variant) is an XOF, not a drop-in SHA-3/SHAKE replacement -- smaller security margin (12 vs 24 rounds) in exchange for speed; needs the XKCP AVX2/AVX-512 target build to hit the stated numbers.
caveats: Numbers are the Keccak team's own marketing page, not a paper or independent benchmark; no compiler or flags stated; the x86 CPU model for the AVX2/AVX-512 figures is unspecified (only 'current Intel architectures'). Most XKCP files are CC0-1.0 but a few third-party files (e.g. brg_endian.h) carry separate permissive licenses -- see the repo LICENSE file.
found_via: GitHub: gh api search/repositories q='keccak XKCP'; benchmark numbers from the linked keccak.team/kangarootwelve.html page

name: Intel ISA-L_crypto (Multi-Buffer / Multi-Hash SHA-256)
baseline: single-buffer SHA-256 implementations of the era (the source whitepaper does not name OpenSSL explicitly, only 'the best known SHA-256 single buffer implementations')
workload: Multi-buffer (Multi-Hash) SHA-256 hashing of a 1 MB buffer on a single core with Hyper-Threading, measured in cycles/byte
claimed_speedup: ~5 cycles/byte for Multi-Hash SHA-256, described as 'over 2x faster than the best known SHA-256 single buffer implementations' (verbatim from the whitepaper)
hardware: Intel Core i7-2600 (Sandy Bridge), single core with Intel HT Technology
stars_or_usage: 302 stars; productized multi-buffer SHA1/SHA256/SHA512/MD5/SM3 used in Intel storage/networking stacks
tradeoffs: Speedup only materializes when batching many independent messages concurrently (multi-buffer); no benefit, and extra complexity, for hashing a single message. Requires NASM and per-ISA assembly build targets (SSE/AVX2/AVX-512/AArch64).
caveats: The only found performance source is a 2012 Intel whitepaper on decade-old hardware (Core i7-2600) that never names OpenSSL directly, just 'best known single buffer implementations' -- baseline naming is inferred, not exact, so baseline_in_list is false and confidence is capped. The repo's own rand_ssl_test.c files test correctness against OpenSSL digests but are not benchmarks, and no modern head-to-head vs current OpenSSL (with SHA-NI) was found in the repo or docs.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/intel/isa-l_crypto (query 'sha256 multi-buffer intel'), then linked wiki whitepaper PDF (multi-hash-paper.pdf) via curl+pdftotext
